chapter: Spontaneity, personality and the flute in jazz
title: Formats for his own music and the flute's place in jazz
summary: Flute and strings, acoustic-electric combinations, work with Earl Stewart, and the flute as a sideline jazz instrument.

blocks.x: Have you found a group of musicians or a format so far that best helps you get your personality out there?

It’s interesting, I do. Sometimes I have some things where I just do flute and strings and I’ve done some concerts like that where I play classical and jazz music combined, some interesting compositions that I’ve done with a friend of mine who teaches at the University of California Santa Barbara, Earl Stewart, who is a great composer and arranger and teacher. And we talked about concepts that combine different idioms. And I have my own group where I just sort of try and combine an acoustic and the electric combination because I think our senses go in that direction. You know we can’t really — we can’t discount the electric. What I mean by that like the synthesizers and that type of sound in a way, you know what I mean? And I try to combine that in certain areas and even deal with things, dealing with vocals and voice, that type of thing. And for me being a flutist, it’s you know, there’s not a lot of flute players. This music didn’t evolve with the flute, saxophone, trumpet combination. You know it was always people like Hubert Laws out there or Herbie Mann or who else am I, I don’t want to leave anybody out, but just the flute is sort of like in its own way a kind of an oddball instrument in jazz. It’s never been really one of those kind of instruments. People like it when they hear it but as © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
a jazz, a bone fide jazz instrument, it’s sort of always been, I think, relegated to like the sideline instrument.
